lead: Pure pursuit aims the missile straight at the target. CLOS keeps it on the launcher-to-target line. Both need only the target's direction, so they are cheap. Both fail to hold the line of sight steady, the real condition for a hit. Early infrared missiles, anti-tank beam riders and short-range surface-to-air systems use them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for guidance families and Chapter 6.3 for the guidance computer.

sections.h3: Line of sight and its rate

blocks.text: The line of sight (LOS) is the straight line from missile to target. Its length R is the range in metres. Its direction changes as either vehicle moves.
The LOS rate λ̇ (lambda dot) is how fast that direction turns, in degrees per second. It is the most useful number in guidance.

If the line joining two vehicles points the same way at every instant, the LOS rate is zero and both are on a collision course: the constant-bearing course. Each runs along a fixed straight line and they meet at the same point at the same time.

blocks.where: λ̇ is the LOS rate in degrees per second. Zero means the LOS direction is frozen.

blocks.text: Any law that does not drive the LOS rate to zero either misses or needs an enormous turn at the end.
Pure pursuit makes the missile's velocity vector point at the target: heading equals LOS direction, lead angle zero.

From behind, this is a tail chase. The missile keeps curving because the target slides sideways, and the LOS rate never reaches zero. Lateral demand is small early and blows up near the end, when a fixed sideways offset must be removed in little time.
Head-on, the path is nearly straight and the demand stays moderate. From the side it curves clearly, though less than in a tail chase, and the terminal demand still rises as the range closes.
Deviated pursuit fixes a lead angle θ greater than zero, aiming ahead. The collision-course lead angle comes from the sine rule.

blocks.where: θ is lead angle between missile velocity and LOS, in degrees; Vt target speed, m/s; Vm missile speed, m/s; β angle between target velocity and LOS, in degrees.

blocks.text: A fixed θ works only while Vt and β stay constant, which they rarely do. Deviated pursuit is a snapshot, not a guidance law.

Command to line of sight (CLOS) keeps the missile on the launcher-to-target line. A tracker at the launcher measures the angle between missile and that line, and the computer sends yaw and pitch commands to cancel the error.

A small angular error at the launcher turns into a linear miss that grows with range, because the same fraction of a degree spans more metres the further out the missile is. The swinging line also demands more lateral acceleration from the missile as range opens.
CLOS suits short-range work: shoulder-launched surface-to-air missiles and ship point defence.

Beam riding is the radar form of CLOS. The launcher points a narrow beam at the target and the missile flies down the beam centre, with a receiver at its tail watching the beam. No target tracker travels in the missile, so it is cheap. The beam widens with distance, limiting range.
Some syllabi call beam riding a separate law; it is CLOS with the beam as reference line.

figure.caption: The missile and target run to a common meeting point, and the line of sight between them is the collision geometry. This straight-line case is a constant-bearing course, not a pure pursuit tail chase.

examples.question: A missile flies at 600 m/s. The target flies at 300 m/s and its velocity makes 60° with the line of sight. Find the lead angle for a collision course, and state what pure pursuit would use instead.
steps: Data: Vm = 600 m/s, Vt = 300 m/s, β = 60°.
Pure pursuit uses θ = 0; the path curves and lateral demand peaks near the end.
examples.answer: The collision-course lead angle is 25.7° ahead of the line of sight, against 0° for pure pursuit.
examples.check:
import math
Vm, Vt = 600.0, 300.0
beta = math.radians(60.0)
s = (Vt/Vm)*math.sin(beta)
theta = math.degrees(math.asin(s))
print(round(s,3), round(theta,1))

traps: Pure pursuit is not a collision course. Only a constant-bearing course has zero LOS rate; in pure pursuit the LOS keeps turning.
λ̇ is an angular rate in degrees per second, not a linear speed in metres per second.
β is measured from LOS to target velocity, not from missile heading or launcher.

CLOS error grows with range because the tracker resolves angles only to a fixed small value: the same fraction of a degree spans a larger linear miss as range opens (and the missile must accelerate harder to stay on the swinging line).
Beam riding is CLOS with the beam as reference. Do not label it homing.

quiz.q: Define the line of sight and the LOS rate.
quiz.a: LOS is the straight line from missile to target, length R. LOS rate λ̇ is how fast that line's direction turns, in degrees per second.
A course on which the LOS direction does not change, so λ̇ = 0 and the two vehicles meet at one point at the same time.

quiz.q: Why does pure pursuit fail to drive the LOS rate to zero?
quiz.a: The missile always points at the target, so its heading follows the LOS instead of holding it. The target's sideways motion keeps turning the LOS; the turn rate is largest near the end.

quiz.q: Vm = 500 m/s, Vt = 250 m/s, β = 90°. Find the lead angle.
Why does CLOS accuracy fall as range increases?
quiz.a: The launcher measures the missile's angular error from the launcher-target line. At long range a given angular resolution spans a larger linear miss at the target, and the missile must stay on a swinging line.

quiz.q: A target is engaged head-on and then from directly behind. Which case curves the missile path more, and why?
quiz.a: The tail chase. The missile closes slowly on a target running away, so it must hold a curve for a long time and lateral demand rises sharply near the end as the remaining offset must be removed in a short closing time. Head-on, paths are nearly straight and closing speed is high.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern short-range air-defence missiles use tracking-aided CLOS, with a predicted intercept point instead of the instantaneous launcher-target line. Beam riders survive in anti-tank missiles and some naval point-defence guns. Pursuit curves are a classic differential-geometry problem, with the tractrix as the equal-speed case.
